en: Re-32583 *Dhyānaślokāḥ*, *Navatriṃśatkalaśakrama*, *Nītisāra*, etc.
(... are used to indicate missing portions, leaf damage, or unidentified characters.
Words/letters within parentheses are my suggestions (based on my understanding).
There are generally six to nine lines per side of each folio. i = image.
May there be auspiciousness! May there be freedom from obstacles! Contemplation.
I praise Gaṇeśa, who has a protruding belly and a dark complexion, holding an axe and a rosary in his two upper hands,
and a ladle and a tusk in his two lower hands, while carrying [the mouse] with his two left hands.

The meditation on Vallabhagaṇapati: [He is] saffron-colored, endowed with four arms, having the face of an elephant and a jeweled casket; holding a goad, a sweetmeat (laḍḍuka), and a tusk, with a beautiful appearance and a joyful countenance—such is the form of Gaṇanātha. (Verse 3)
One should meditate upon [the deity] whose hands hold a citron, a mace, a discus, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, and grain;
whose hand-lotuses are raised with an elephant-goad, a jewel, and a vase;
who is accompanied by his beloved, who holds a lotus and a makara, and who is adorned with radiant ornaments.
The Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa), who effects the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the universe, bestows desired objects.

Shining with ornaments such as armlets and girdles inlaid with fresh gems, she possesses the luster of pearls, wears divine garments, and is adorned with musk-paste, betel-leaves, and garlands of white lotuses.

I bow to Śrī Lakṣmī, whose face is fragrant with the scent of camphor, whose lotus-eyes are full of compassion, who holds a lotus in her hand, and who dwells in the heart of her honored Lord, for the sake of universal prosperity.
[Now follows] the meditation on Siddhi, Buddhi, and Gaṇapati.
He is radiant, possessing the face of a beautiful elephant, flawless, and among the skillful...
1), bearing a hundred [rays] like the sun, blazing with a crown.
I worship the god Gaṇeśa, whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire, who brings about auspiciousness, who sits upon a lotus, and who is endowed with supreme perfection and wisdom.
The meditation for the attainment of success:
[one should meditate on] the goddess Siddhidā, white in complexion, holding a beautiful lotus in her right hand and a bright rosary in her left;
she has long, hanging arms, large eyes, and stands to the left of Vighneśa.
I worship the goddess Siddhi, who has moon-like countenance, whose feet are worshipped by the gods, who sits upon a throne, and who is adorned with armlets, necklaces, and ornaments.
To the right [of Vighneśa] is the goddess Buddhi;

she is yellow in complexion, holds a vessel of cooked food (pākaja), is radiant with jeweled earrings on her ears, has long-hanging ear-lobes, possesses a gracious countenance, and stands to the right of Vighneśa.
I worship the goddess Śrī-Buddhi, who is adorned with strings of pearls, possesses two eyes, is divine and exquisitely decorated, and whose pair of lotus feet are praised by the gods.
To Pañcamukhagaṇapati: (l.
7) He who possesses hands granting fearlessness and boons, holding a noose, a tusk, a rosary, an axe, a sword, a mallet, a severed head, a mace, and a vessel of water;
he who is the preeminent lion with five elephant faces.
May he whose complexion is as beautiful as gold, named Heramba, protect [us].
The meditation on the mantra of Māṇikyavācaka.

I bow to him whose body bears a single face, two arms, a rosary in the right hand, and a book and a vessel of prosperity in the left hand; whose body wears ornaments and a garland of Rudrākṣas; and whose nature is like that of the wind.
Right Concentration.
White in luster, with jewel-like locks and a topknot, gentle and serene of countenance; his right hand is long with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), while his left holds a vessel of nectar.
He is Śiva, established in the lotus of Nirvāṇa, the destroyer of the Buddhist [heresy].
I worship the excellent poet Nānādrāviḍa, the crest-jewel among teachers, whose composition is known as *Jñāna*.
To him [who is] Rudrakṣadāmaśiva: one whose limbs are adorned with the feet of Śiva, who has a gentle countenance, and whose ear-ornaments bear the auspicious marks of Śiva.
With palms joined in reverence, holding a blade of grass in his left arm, with a gentle smile, the sage, the lord of eloquent speech...
The Subrahmaṇyā meditation:
she has four arms; the left hands hold a rosary and the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*), while the right [hands hold] a lotus and a vessel full of coral.
To the slayer of the demon Tāraka, the one whose vehicle is a peacock, the commander of the divine army, the god... the teacher of the world; (l.

3) the six-faced one, whose vehicle is a peacock, the three-eyed one adorned with variegated garments; holding a spear, a thunderbolt, a sword, a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, a shield, and a bow. (l. 4)

One should always meditate upon Skanda, the son of Śiva, who is superior to the gods, bestowing the fulfillment of all desires, and holding a peacock, a goad, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*),

and a lotus. I worship the goddess Senānī, who stands to the left [of Skanda], who is dark-complexioned, holds a blue lotus, is adorned with divine garments and ornaments, has a long hanging hand, wears garlands of *mandāra* flowers, whose sandals are worshipped by the gods, whose face is like the moon, who is decorated with strings of pearls, possesses two eyes, and has three folds on her belly.

The meditation (dhyāna) on Vallīśvarī: I meditate upon her who is yellow in complexion, holding a blue lotus, radiant with a jeweled earring, with a long garland hanging from her right side, wearing a crown adorned with a tiara, her breasts covered by a fine bodice,
gazing at one another [with her consort], white-complexioned to the left of the one born in the Śara forest (Kārttikeya), and wearing a garland shining like jasmine flowers.
Śaśimukhī and Vallīśvarī are the two objects of meditation.
The Meditation on Mayūra:
Seated upon a variegated lion-throne, with a face raised up by serpents, possessing great strength and a massive body—to that Mayūra I bow.
The Meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
The Rudrākṣa, whose hand is fire, together with the Lord of the Urdhva; the seat of eternal radiance, accompanied by the Fire-god, carrying the Gaṅgā;
Śiva, the syllable Om, the root mantra, accompanied by the sages, the essence of the Vedas, the Gaṅgā of Śiva.
I bow to the Lord of Kailāsa, the sovereign of all the gods, the deity Dakṣiṇāmūrtti.
The meditation on Somaskanda:

Kṛṣṇa has his left leg bent and resting while he sleeps; he holds a deer and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in his lower right hands, and [bestows] boons (*vara*) in his upper [hands]... [granting them] from the left.
I worship that Lord of Guha, who stands in the center together with the Goddess, whose other foot is supported by his left arm as she sleeps, and who holds a lotus in his hand.
Meditation on the Form of Sadāśiva:
Seated upon a peaceful lotus throne, wearing a crown of the moon, possessing five faces and three eyes,
he holds in his right hands a trident, a vajra, a discus, a sword, an axe, and the gesture of fearlessness, while [holding] a serpent in his left hand.
In his left [hands], he holds a serpent, a noose, a bell adorned with ornaments, and a goad;
he is endowed with various ornaments and has a crystal-like... (line 2) ...he should have eyes like the fire at the tip of a finger, resembling the moon.
The four guardians of the directions, beginning with Paṅkaja and Abhaya,
should be adorned with various ornaments including snakes.
They possess lofty crowns, are radiant, and have the nature of the Transmental (An-uttara).
Having the luster of vermilion, three-eyed, bearing the digit of the nectar-moon, riding upon a bull, clad in red garments,
her breasts heavy with the weight of their fullness, having attained the onset of youth, adorned with various ornaments, dwelling in a lotus, her form infused with the seed-syllable— [I bow to her].
I bow to the Goddess, who is enriched with noose and goad, whose hands grant fearlessness and boons, and who is the source of the universe; I bow to you, the Supreme Sovereign,
who is dark-hued, two-eyed, two-armed, and possessed of graceful gestures, with your feet placed in a curved posture right and left,
with your hand holding the tip of a bracelet that has the luster of a blue lotus, and who hangs down from the mountain.
The meditation on Naṭeśa:
He has one face, four arms, and three eyes; in his left [hands] he holds a *dhudhūraka* flower and the moon; his hands hold a peacock feather and a lotus; and his right foot is bent upward.
Wearing an auspicious svastika on his left [arm] and earrings, he holds a ḍamaru drum and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I perpetually salute Naṭeśa, whose matted locks are disheveled, who stands upon the body of the enemy of Śambhu’s ashes.
The Meditation on Kṣetrapāla:
[One should meditate upon him] bearing matted locks of red flames, wearing the moon, possessing a body of red luster,
holding in his hands a trident, a noose, and a ḍamaru drum, and acting as the protector of the world.

I bow to the auspicious Kṣetrapāla Vaṭuka, the lord of Bhūtas and Piśācas, who is Nirvāṇa, whose vehicle is the dog, the three-eyed one, and who causes a tumultuous joy. [This concludes] the meditation on Bālasubrahmaṇya.
I worship the one with a single face and two eyes, who holds two lotuses in his two hands, who acts for the benefit of the Brahmins, who possesses the form of a child and the radiance of the sun;
the god who bears the king of weapons, the *ṛk*-verse, the deer, and the chisel, and who is adorned by the moon upon his forehead.
One should meditate upon the goddess Umāmaheśvarī and the King of Weapons (Astrarāja).
For the devotee, [one should visualize] a single foot, two faces, and three eyes; adorned with a line of hair like a *darbha* grass rope;
white-bodied, with a parrot-like nose; and seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) in the form of a staff.

To the one reclining with the beautiful Śrīmīnākṣī, who is peaceful, seated upon a lotus throne, resembling the sun, with the moon as his crest-jewel, and possessing three eyes... (I.9a, l.1) ...to him who is tranquil, seated on a lotus throne, resembling the sun, with the moon as his crest-jewel, and possessing three eyes.
May Maheśa, who holds a lotus, a trident, fire, and a rosary in his right hands,
and likewise displays the gesture of granting boons in the left— joined with Gaurī and seated in a posture of bliss— manifest before me.
He is seated in the meditative posture of Sukhāsana,
with his right hand resting upon his left leg which is drawn up; he is dark blue in color, holding a deer, a sword, a battle-axe,
and a boon-granting gesture, while wearing bracelets and a waist-cloth.
I worship the Lord of Umā and Guha, joined in the center by the Goddess whose other two feet are resting upon his left side,
and accompanied by Skanda with his two lotus-like hands.
The meditation on Somaskanda:
[He is] peaceful, seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown bearing the moon, five-faced, and three-eyed;
he holds in his right hands a trident, a vajra, a sword, an axe, and the gesture of fearlessness.
In the left portion, [he holds] a nāga, a noose, a bell, the fire of universal destruction, and a goad.
I bow to the Lord of Pārvatī, who is adorned with various ornaments and resembles a crystal gem. (Verse 2) This is the meditation on Caṇḍeśvara:
holding a *ṭaṅka* in his hand of protection (*abhaya-hasta*) and granting boons (*varada*) with his other two hands, he is reclining with his feet hanging down.
Adorned with all ornaments, wearing the sacred thread and a topknot, he has the Brahmā-voice and a fierce roar.
The Meditation on the Bull:
The bull is said to have the form of the four-footed Vedas; its two horns are the form of Agni; it has three eyes, which are the Sun;
its face is the deity Rudra; and its teeth are the lunar mansions (nakṣatras)—such is the form described as the Bull.
I salute Skanda, who has one face and two eyes, whose two hands hold two lotuses, who acts for the welfare of brahmins, who possesses the form of a child, and who shines with the splendor of the sun.
The meditation on the rat (*mūṣika*):
likewise, [he is] red-eyed with beautiful fangs, possessing a sharp tail and four legs, and is [seated upon] a tortoise.
l.1) (Side heading) Consisting of Śiva.
Salutation to Gaṇapati.
The sequence of thirty-nine pitchers.
Salutations to the illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas.

The fourth is the door-pitcher (*dvārakumbha*), the eight pitchers for the gatekeepers (*dvārapālāṣṭakumbhaka*), and the ten for the world-protectors (*lokapālādaśa*). Between Indra, Agni, and Bhānu (the Sun) is the Vāstu-pitcher; in the south-west (*nairṛtya*) is the Astra-pitcher, in the north-west (*vāyavyā*) the Kṣetrapāla-pitcher, and in the north-east (*īśāna*) the Guru-pitcher. Together with the [other] pitchers in the six directions, there is the Astra and the Astravardhani. Upon the altar (*vedikā*), in the center, are Sadāśiva and Anomanī; likewise, from the east to the north-east, are the pitchers for the eight Vidyeśvaras. Thus, there are ninety-three pitchers specifically for the initiation sacrifice (*dīkṣāmakha*).

The procedure for the worship of the twenty-seven jars (*saptaviṃśatikalaśapūjākrama*), the pacification of the Sun (*sūryaśānti*), the auspicious time (*suri*), the subsequent period (*anukala*), the cessation of breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and the time of joy (*nandīkāla*); [the lords of the months: Śukra, the Boar-faced one (*varāha*), Taurus (*vṛṣa*), Bāhuleya, Devī, Caṇḍa, Vāstu, Lakṣmī, the Wreath-wielder (*vallarīdhara*), Fire (*vahni*), Kāla, the Lord of Waters (*jaleśa*), Wind (*vāyu*), Śrīda, Maheśa, Viṣṇu, Hari, Gaṇapa, and the Preceptor (*guru*)—these are the twenty-seven.
The sequence of the abiding of the vase.

One should worship Bṛhānandi and Śānti in order at the north of the eastern gate; Mahākāla and Vajrin to the south; Bhānu and Agni to the east of the southern gate; then Bhṛṅgin and Vidya; Vināyaka, Yama, Brahmā, and Nirṛti in order; Viṣṇu, Vṛṣa, and Nivṛtti to the south of the western gate; Skanda, Varuṇa, Lakṣmī, and Vāyu in sequence; and one should worship Vighneśa, Caṇḍa, Kubera, Guru, and Īśāna in order at the north of the western gate.
He states the characteristics of the pavilion:

In the sacrifice... [one should fashion] the one who grants fearlessness and boons, [residing in] an empty grove, [and] the eight... by means of hands fashioned by Bhāskara, according to the prescribed characteristics.
He states the extent of the altar for the previously mentioned pavilions.

Endowed with one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight *rasas* (flavors/elements), and fashioned from heavy materials each measuring eight finger-breadths in height at the center; resembling a sacrificial altar (*vedi*) or a mirror, seated upon a square base, it is then rolled into a pill (*vaṭī*) possessing the qualities of the moon and shining like the moonlight.
He states the general characteristics of all fire-pits (kuṇḍas), such as the square and others, by way of their common form.
The pit is equal in width and depth, joined with a rim above;

it has one cubit [in height] externally by means of fingers [measuring] four, three, and two [units], respectively. That pit is provided with a navel in the middle, measuring half of that [height], shaped like a pipal leaf, and granting sons; its neck is considered to be one unit less [than the height].
The determination of the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*), the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and so forth:

during the annual period, in the month of Pauṣa—excluding Caitra—during a festival of the deity, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, during eclipses, and on the day of the ancestors (*pitṛtithi*); under the asterisms of Anurādhā, Svāti, Mṛgaśiras, Maghā, Nirṛti (Mūla), Pūṣan (Puṣya), Śravaṇa, Jyeṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttaras; and excluding Tuesday and Sunday.
Initiation (*dīkṣā*)... [is] the time for battle.

Excluding the fourth, ninth, sixth, eighth, fourteenth, and full moon days, on the remaining auspicious days, the sacrifice brings joy, long life, good fortune, splendor, and auspiciousness. Also, *sukarman*, *dhṛti*... and *harṣa*... and *aindra*, as well as the sixteen *bava*, *bālava*, and *karṇa-kaulabha* [tithis], are auspicious.
Now the *lagna* is being discussed: ... [it is] auspicious and excellent for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

When pierced by the female planets (the signs of the zodiac), both [types of houses] become fixed; when pierced by the malefic planets, they move with a base nature. When pierced by the benefic planets, they are gentle, increasing the meaning of the house-lines and leading to dharma and existence. Having abandoned the state of Agastya (the star Canopus) in the moon... the malefic planets situated in the seventh house cause distress, while the auspicious planets in the eighth house purify the house.

At the equinoxes, at both solstices, on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, during festivals of Umā, when performing initiations (*dīkṣā*), and during auspicious rites, initiation is auspicious on the bright fortnight or on a pure lunar festival (*parvan*). In the dark fortnight, it should be performed before midday. For the installation (*sthāpana*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), initiation, Śivarātri, and the festival of Śiva, it should be done according to the solar calendar. However, according to the lunar calendar, it should be performed on a lunar day (*tithi*) free from defects—specifically the second, third, fifth, or especially the sixth; or the twelfth may be used, or even the thirteenth.

These are declared to be the favorable days for the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*): among the weekdays, Monday, Friday, Wednesday, and Thursday are most excellent; Wednesday is the best. Regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), they say those other than these two—Sunday and Monday—are suitable; one should perform the rite of initiation under Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury. As for the lunar mansions, Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, the three *Uttarās*, Puṣya, and Śatabhiṣaj are recommended.

The asterisms are said to be the three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Maghā, Mūla, Revatī, Abhijit, and Śravaṇa. For the auspicious sacrifice (śivayāga), according to the rule for the fourteen zodiac signs, one should take Taurus, Virgo, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius, Gemini, or Libra, or else Sagittarius, Pisces, [Cancer], or [Aries]. Thus he describes the characteristics of the pavilion (maṇḍapa).

The ground for the door, however, should consist of sixteen, sixteen, nine, and nine squares [respectively] by means of the six, five, and four [units]. In the middle, there should be three squares for the central altar, and nine and five [squares] for the *kuṇḍa*; such is the procedure for the temple (*maṇḍapa*) of Śiva.
(l.4) The ritual for the Śiva-vessel (*śivakumbha*).

I shall describe the method for the auspicious water-pot (*śivakumbha*); listen, O Nandikeśvara! The belly is said to be twenty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width and is declared to be shaped like the ocean; it is called "Āham" because it is three times that [width]. The neck has a height of eight finger-breadths and a width of one *kauśika-aṅgula*; the lip is said to be one finger-broad, and its protrusion is three [finger-breadths] thick.

This is declared to be the *śivakumbha*; in the same way, one should fashion other jars (*kumbhakas*), and for the *vardhinīs*, half of that [size]. For the *kuṇḍikā* jar, one should have it made with half-remnants joined, possessing a split, a crack, a hole, and white discoloration.

One should avoid that which is blue, burnt, or ancient. A full *kuṇḍika* contains two *khāris* of water; [the medium size] is one less *khārī*, while the lowest is filled with one *droṇa*. For the two *śivakumbhas*, it increases by half a *droṇa*; the measurements for the *kalaśa* increase by half a *droṇa* for the *vardhanī*. The deities [are assigned] to the *kumbha* and the others.
Kumbha, Śiva, Mukhordra, Madhya, Viṣṇu, and likewise Prajāpati on the back; Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī in the belly, and Nadī and Kālī at the two sides—these are their jar-deities.
This is the form of the jar.

Having placed the *ghaṭa* (pot), one should place the *māṃsa* (flesh); water is traditionally known as *rakta* (blood). The wise one should place *rakta* (blood) and the *asthi* (bone), as well as the *sūtra* (thread) and the *nāḍī* (channel). That which is called *vastra* (cloth) is [placed] with the *nalikā* (tube) and the head; it is joined with the *dha...hva*. The *cūta* (mango) is traditionally said to be born from the leaf. This is indeed the sevenfold placement (*saptanyāsa*), the life-force of the mantra, Sadāśiva. Regarding the characteristic of the thread: there are three threads for the wrapping around the *kumbha* (vessel), two threads for the *karaka* (small jar), and for all others, there is one thread.

One should wrap it. The best of teachers should wrap it according to the very rite of the Armor (*kavaca*). The best [thread] is the size of a sesame seed; the middling is the size of a barley grain; the inferior has the appearance of an elephant’s eye, possessing the characteristics described for the thread of the *kumbha*.
This is the characteristic of the *darbha* grass.

Kuśa, kāśa, uśīra, ... likewise with *vrīhi*, as well as *viśvāmitra* and *mauñjī*—these are proclaimed as the seven types of darbha grass. First, with *kuśa* and *kāśa*; second, *viśvāmitra*; third, *mauñjī*; fourth, from *kāśa* and *darbha*; fifth, *uśīra* and *darbha*; sixth, with *vaidarbha*; seventh, with *yava* and *dūrvā*. Thus are the seven types of darbha proclaimed, beginning with *kuśa*...

The *brahmā* [grass] is the first; likewise, *viśvāmitra* is the second; the *mauñjī* is the third; the fourth belongs to both the tenth [and the preceding]; the fifth consists of *śīra-darbhas*; the sixth is the *vaidarbha*; the seventh is that which is *yava*; likewise, *dūrvā* is declared as the seventh type of *darbha*, and similarly, from *kuśa* and *brahmā*, *viśvāmitra* is the second, and the *mauñjī* is indeed [the third].

From that [Darbha grass] comes Viśvāmitra the king; from Kāśa come Vaiśyas, and from Dūrvā come Śūdras; from Yava come the Uttara and other castes, and from Dūrvā likewise... (l. 2) a woman is thick at the tip, a neuter is thick at the base, and a male Darbha has a root equal to its tip—such is the characteristic of Darbha. Regarding the deities of the Darbha and others: Brahmā resides at the root of the Kuśa, Keśava in the middle, and Śaṅkara is said to be at the tip; these are declared to be the presiding deities of the Kuśa grass.

A woman [is associated with] the festivals of consecration and so forth; at the time of initiation, a man [should go]; the funeral rite is to be known as neuter—these are the characteristics of the *darbha* grass.
The characteristics of the purifier (pavitra).

The tip [of the *pavitra*] should be four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long, the knot (*granthi*) one finger-breadth, and the ring (*valaya*) likewise one finger-breadth; such is the characteristic of the *pavitra*. Regarding the deities of the *pavitra*: Brahmā and the others are the deities of the knot, Viṣṇu is the deity of the ring, and Maheśvara is the deity of the *pavitra*. Just as Indra’s [weapon] is the thunderbolt (*vajra*), the trident (*triśūla*), and the discus (*hiraṇya-cakra*), so too is the *pavitra* of Viṣṇu. One should perform the rite of sipping water (*ācamana*) while holding the *pavitra* in the hand. One should know that the fivefold [rite] is for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and the fourfold is for malevolent magic (*abhicāraka*).

Having performed the rite of pacification (*śānti*) with three *darbha* blades, and that for the gods and ancestors with two *darbha* blades—one should thus properly perform the purification (*pavitra*). One should perform the ritual according to the distinction of the acts using two *darbha* blades; this is the characteristic of the *kūrca*. Regarding the reception of guests and the offering to the ancestors, the *kūrca* made of *darbha* blades should be equal to sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), with a pair of finger-breadths at the tip... [the middle one] has been described... as the *kūrca*. (l. 3) One should know that the best consists of nine *kāśa* blades, the middle of seven *kāśa* blades, and the lowest of five *kāśa* blades; such is the threefold characteristic of the *kūrca*. (l. 4)

A chariot-shaped [seat] with its tip pointing upward is declared to bestow nourishment; one with the tip pointing downward brings about pacification. An inner seat (*kūrca*) made of *darbha* grass should be prepared for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*). A man should use a *kūrca* made of *darbha*; likewise, a woman uses a *vardhanī* made of *darbha*. One should prepare a seat (*viṣṭara*) for a neuter person. Furthermore, a man should hold the purifier (*pavitra*) in his hand.

The half-verse for the seat (*viṣṭara*) is as follows: "Straight [blades] from the *palāśa* tree, measuring that [same length], called *parimya*, sixteen finger-breadths in size, serving as sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), and a span (*prādeśa*) in measure. Regarding the *kūrca*: the presiding deity of the *kūrca* is Sarasvatī; the knot of the *kūrca* is [Sarasvatī]; the tip of the *kūrca* is... [etc. (I.15a, l. 1).

The deity of the *sāvitrī* is Bhūmi. A seat (*viṣṭara*) consists of an uncounted number of dark-green darbha blades, reaching the length of the arms, with their tips even and their knots tied together. A seat joined with thirty-six darbha blades is proclaimed as the best; the middle is twenty-five; the eighth is sixteen; and the lowest is eight. Such is the characteristic of a seat measuring the length of the arms.
The sword of wisdom.

One should fashion a sword of knowledge from thirty-six *darbha* blades; its tip should be four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long, and its hilt half that measure. It should be provided with a handle one palm-length in size for the purpose of grasping it in the hand. In the middle, it should be four finger-breadths wide, and below that, it is said to be two finger-breadths.

In the same manner, for the characteristics of the effigy joined with the tail, one should take thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass; having made the tip four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long and two finger-breadths as the double knot, this should represent the influence of the head, and three finger-breadths should be made for the measurement of the neck. On both the left and right sides, there should be five blades of *darbha* each, totaling eighteen finger-breadths. From the arm down to the wrist, the measurement is six finger-breadths.

But this remaining foot [of the sacrificial post] should be made in the battle [of construction] neither with the hand nor with finger-breadths; rather, one should fashion the middle section joined with twenty-six *darbha* blades. The heart[-section] should be fifteen finger-breadths, and likewise two parts of that *darbha* should be eight finger-breadths. This is declared to be the thigh and knee; now hear of the shank in finger-breadths: this remaining foot should be six finger-breadths in measure, as is the *paridhi*. The *paridhi*, however, is measured by the span of the mother’s hand (*mātṛ-hasta*). The fuel-stick (*samit*)...

The *samit* (sacrificial fuel stick) is said to be the smallest [of the three], twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, moist, and free from hollows or cracks. It should be taken from trees suitable for sacrificial wood. The fuel sticks should be twelve finger-breadths long; if they belong to beings of a passionate (*rājasa*) or dark (*tāmasa*) nature, one should avoid those that are crooked or have split tips. This constitutes an ancillary part of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

First is the fragrant oil, second the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), third the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and fourth the bath with ghee; fifth is the bath with milk, sixth the bath with curd, seventh the bath with honey, eighth likewise the essence of sugarcane, ninth the water of boiled rice, tenth the coconut water, and eleventh the fragrant [water]... the twelfth bathing shall be [the final one].
The characteristics of a gemstone.

The presiding deities of the bell are as follows: for the jewels, Vāsudeva; for the tongue, Sarasvatī; the staff is said to belong to Bhāskara (the Sun); the trident to the Threefold Form (Trimūrti); the sound is said to be Śiva; and the bell itself has these as its presiding deities. Upon hearing the sound of the bell, there is the destruction of the Rākṣasas. Asuras, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and other Rākṣasas flee far away at the sound of the jewel, especially to a great distance.

The essence of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) consists of grape juice, sugar-cane juice, the essence of flowers, cow’s milk, and clarified butter; this is known as the *pañcāmṛta*. Furthermore, the *pañcāmṛta* of the Piśācas is known to consist of sugar, honey, plantain fruit, cow’s clarified butter, and coconut.
In another scripture.

One should repeatedly wash the flowers and fruits offered to the Lord—bilva, tulasī, dhūrdhara, kalhāra, and other blossoms. By worshipping with these, one is purified even of the sin of killing a Brahmin; likewise, *droṇaka* for killing a cow, *śvetārka* for killing a preceptor, and *dūrvā* for killing a preceptor; *svarṇasteya* (theft of gold) with *phalāśa*, *liṅgacheda* (severing the linga) with *aśokaka*, drinking liquor with *karṇikāra*, and the sin of stealing weapons with worship using [these].

Adultery with another’s wife, the faults arising from marriage, the wearing of garlands [by those unfit], and the fruits of evil speech; the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the killing of one’s mother, the slaughter of deer, and indeed adultery with another’s wife—these are the enemies of the family of the Lord of the Liṅga.

A man who has committed single sins, or who worships with sesame, *dūrvā* grass, and unhusked rice (*akṣata*) during bad dreams or ill omens, or who has gone to another’s wife—by worshipping the Supreme Lord (*Parameśāna*) together with these [substances] for the sake of removing that fault, there shall be the fruit of eleven [sins]. One should not worship on the equinoxes (*viṣuva*) or at the solstices (*saṃkrānti*). On the day of the sun’s entry into a zodiac sign (*mārīkṣaka*), one should worship the Supreme Lord together with sesame, *dūrvā*, and unhusked rice to destroy faults; there shall be the fruit of eleven. Therefore, with great effort, one should worship with sesame, *dūrvā*, and unhusked rice.
Rudrākṣa, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel, and fruit;

unbroken rice (*akṣata*) for the destruction of enemies, and flowers for sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Incense removes sins, the lamp destroys death, and from the food offering one obtains a kingdom; betel [bestows] inexhaustible [wealth]. Durvā grass, unbroken rice, and bilva fruit; durvā grass, sandalwood, and *āsīdhyūrdhya*—unbroken rice is for desired objects, the bilva fruit is for liberation (*mokṣa*), and the three kinds of fruit likewise [grant these].

The *bilva* fruit represents the powers of will, knowledge, and action; the moon is the three leaves of the *bilva*. By the mere sight, touch, or even the praise of a *bilva* leaf, the sin committed by a priest (*ṛtvij*) is destroyed—of this there is no doubt. One should worship Girijā with even dried *bilva* leaves, O Nārada; one is liberated from all sins. The *bilva*...

One should worship the single Liṅga with unbroken leaves; for him who is thus liberated from all sins, the world of Śiva awaits. A three-petaled leaf, shaped according to the three *guṇas*... (line 2) ...and a trident-shaped bilva leaf, which destroys the sins of three births—this is the singular worship of Śiva with the bilva.
If the essence of policy dwells within a man whose heart regards [only] his own happiness...
Having cultivated this disposition, one should always worship [the Buddha]. (1.2)
One should speak exactly as gods, Brahmins, teachers, ancestors, and those wearing sectarian marks speak when they address one in their dreams. (3)
For one who has no son, there is no destination, nor indeed heaven, nor even [liberation].
Therefore, having beheld the face of a son, one may become an ascetic for the last time. (3.4)
The moon is the lamp of the night, the sun is the illuminator of dawn;
Dharma is the lamp of the three worlds, and the son is the lamp of the lineage. (4)
Coconut trees do not provide for men that small amount of water drunk in early youth which, when remembered, is placed upon the head as a cooling burden;
rather, they grant a life-sustaining gift that is like nectar.
For the virtuous do not remember an injury that has been done to them.
What indeed does a wise person not accomplish when impelled by the fear of his own hands?
For the intellect of human beings is already directed toward action. (6)
What merit is there in being good toward those who do one good? But for him who is good even toward those who do him harm—that is what is called true goodness by the wise. (7)
The moon wanes; it is by nature subject to transformation, a mine of defects such as spots, at the time of its final phase.
Nevertheless, it is constantly borne upon the head by Hara;
for the great have no concern with the merits or faults of those who have sought refuge.
...and even Viṣṇu himself, the wielder of the uneven weapon (the trident), was likewise burnt by the All-pervading Lord; by whom then can the natural order be transgressed? (9)
One should avoid from afar the section on great rivers, the subjugation of great men, and that which is pierced by the masses. 10.
In conduct, one should never act like women crossing a full river, like those whose feet [are sinking], like a friendship with a serpent, or like the words of a merchant. (11)
Disobedience to kings, the humiliation of the honor of Brahmins, and sleeping on separate beds—these are said to be weapons for women even without a blade. (12)
The king is proclaimed by the seers to be composed of all the gods;
therefore, one should look upon him as such, for purity does not arise from treating him otherwise. 13.
Those who, without a machine, a mantra, or even a loom,
deceive men and women— by that very act they steal away their wisdom and wealth.
(14) The mind of a man is unsteady, and his fortune is either deficient or excessive.
Even the god Varṣaṇa does not know this, much less a human being. 15.
An earthquake portends misfortune for both the king and his virtuous ministers;

likewise, a comet is declared to be the destruction of the monarch. (16) They say that poison is not truly poison; it is the property of a Brahmin that is called poison. Poison is but a single [instance].
By what does one kill? The property of a Brahmin is called poison; it destroys even sons and grandsons. 17.
Learning, truth, austerity, virtue, wisdom, wealth, and high status—having entered the fire of women, the fool consumes all these as if they were fuel. (18)

Who has seen or heard of a crow possessing a fine crest, a eunuch being truthful in speech, a hermaphrodite possessing heroism, a drunkard possessing a mind focused on reality, one who observes everything possessing patience, or a king possessing the pacification of desire? (19)

In the forest, in battle, in the midst of enemies, water, or fire, upon the great ocean or on the peak of a mountain—whether one is heedless, distracted, or standing still—merits performed in the past protect him. (20)
O playful one, [you are] the satisfying [of desires], not poison... (I.19a, l.1).
Together with the Nāgas, the gods, and the hosts of yogins, one should not harbor hatred toward Brahman. 21.
Having performed [this] on one side... (l.2).
On the other side is the protection of the life of a living being who is terrified by fear. 22.

Those who betray trust and those who kill those who have sought refuge dwell in a terrible hell as long as the moon and sun exist. (23) He who betrays a friend, he who withholds a promised gift, and he who is a betrayer of trust—
Those fools who go to hell, even as they [speak] regarding the moon and the sun;
(24) lifespan, wealth, the positions of the planets, the application of mantras and medicines, generosity, and honor and dishonor—these nine are always to be guarded in secret. (25)

That which is muttered with the tip of a finger, that which is muttered while jumping about, and that which is muttered with a distracted mind— these three kinds of recitation shall be fruitless. (26) In this world, a virtuous person is able to point out the faults of others as easily as they can enumerate all their virtues.
A virtuous and truthful person is able to point out the faults of others while remaining focused on their own good qualities.
(i.19b, l.1) The deity does not exist in wood, nor in stone or clay; for existence [itself] is the deity. Therefore, existence is indeed the cause. 28. (l.2)
In mantras, sacred fords, brahmins, deities, astrologers, medicines, and teachers—
whatever the disposition toward these may be, let success therein be under one's control.
(29) They provide shade for others while they themselves remain in the scorching heat.
And they bear fruit even after millions of aeons, not for their own sake—such is the nature of the virtuous.
(30) Rivers flow for the benefit of others; fire burns for the benefit of others;
trees bear fruit for the benefit of others; and the splendors of the righteous exist for the benefit of others. (31)
Enterprise, daring, fortitude, intelligence, power, and valor—
these six qualities abide in him who...
Even a god fears this. 32.
He gives, he receives, he tells a secret, he asks, he eats...
[the characteristic of a kinsman]. // 33 //
And so it is said: "Fortune herself desires to dwell with those who are wise, not procrastinating, skilled in the knowledge of action, unattached to sense objects, heroic, and firm in resolve. (34)

On the mountain are peacocks; in the sky, the mass of clouds; in the water, the sun; on the earth, the lotuses—those two who possess such splendor worthy of these [beauties] cause the lilies to wither far away.
In this essence-less saṃsāra, the essence is the deer-eyed woman.

"Half of that half... [and so on]. But what is the use of wealth when one has abandoned the [cycle of] rebirth? (36) Having reflected that in this essence-less saṃsāra there are those who are the very essence, the King, desiring the beautiful woman, bestowed half of his own body upon her. (37)

Having given gifts according to his means, having worshipped the Linga of Śūnya, and having constantly protected those who depend upon him, the king shall obtain the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. 38.
Just as a tiny seed of the *nyagrodha* tree, when placed in fertile soil,
attains great expansion, so too does a gift bestowed upon a worthy recipient [grow].
(39) Wealth entrusted to an excellent recipient brings about great merit for the donor.
Just as water in the ocean produces a pearl within a pearl-oyster, so too [the king’s favor] produced the state of being a pearl for the cloud-like Pāyodha.

(40) But the King—his hands stained red with blood, desiring the fruit [of his actions], and seeking a friend—did not look upon the royal preceptor, the astrologer, especially not the one who was his well-wisher. (41)
One whose hands are stained with blood shall not behold his beloved wife, his dear friend, nor even his youngest son; likewise [he shall not see] his lord. (42)
Cows see by scent; the twice-born see by means of the Veda; [the others] see by means of their eyes.
By means of his two eyes, the others conquer. || 43 ||
The cage-like body of mortals is perpetually afflicted by the diseases of all the gods, is the abode of the impurities of all the gods, and is always filled with suffering. 44.
By those very [deeds], an infinite fruit has been secured by those performers of meritorious actions; yet for them, through birth, the body is divided between self and others. (45)

Those who possess neither learning nor austerity, neither generosity nor moral conduct, nor virtue nor righteousness—they are merely a burden upon the world of mortals; they wander on earth as beasts in human form. (46)
Of what use is a noble lineage to an embodied being who is destitute of learning? One who lacks noble birth, if possessed of knowledge, is honored even by the gods. (47)
Like a mother she protects; like a father she enjoins one to what is beneficial; and having removed [obstacles], she causes one to delight in what is lovely.
She spreads her fame throughout the quarters; what, indeed, does she not accomplish, like a wish-fulfilling creeper?
Knowledge. 48.
The king is the kinsman of those without kin; the king is the eye of the sightless.
The king is both father and mother; the king is the teacher of conduct. To those half-dead there is neither teacher nor kinsman; for those consumed by passion there is neither fear nor shame.
For those afflicted by anxiety there is no happiness; for those afflicted by the desire for sleep there is neither pleasure nor the right time [for it]. (50)
Manu has declared that both parents when aged, a wife, and a son who is an infant— even if he has committed a hundred improper acts— must be maintained.
But that woman who is bereft of her husband, even if she possesses sons and is fully replete with wealth and grain, is called a widow by the wise. (52)

When one has a friend whose mind is constant, a servant who possesses virtues, a wife who conducts herself well and is sweet-spoken, and a mind of friendship, one indeed becomes happy by confiding one's sorrows to them. (53)
It is truly marvelous that your son is solely intent on benefiting others; for sandalwood trees do not produce the perception of coolness in their own bodies. // 54 //
That man who is engaged in the activity of benefiting others attains the highest prosperity on earth,
as well as other supreme attainments. (55) The suffering that arises for a person at the thought "I shall die"—

By that [means], one may infer that another person has also been protected by him. (56) One should protect wealth even at the cost of one's wife; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth; but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (57)
One should not grieve for what is past, nor should one worry about the future; the wise conduct themselves only in relation to present affairs. (58)
That which is to become becomes; thus, for example, a coconut must become [ripe].
That which is to go goes.
Always like the intellect of one whose mind has been consumed by an elephant. 59.

Dead is the gift to a poor man; dead is the sacrifice performed by one who has not purchased [the Soma]; dead is the gift to those ignorant of the Vedas; dead is sexual union that results in no offspring. (60)
Bodies are impermanent, and worldly prosperity is never eternal;
death is ever-present, therefore one must practice the accumulation of Dharma.
(61) Listen to the entirety of the essence of Dharma as it has been taught by millions of scriptures.

Benefiting others leads to merit; harming others leads to sin. (62) Agriculture, knowledge, trade, a wife, wealth, sovereignty, and prosperity—all these must be maintained with great firmness, O Kṛṣṇa, as if they were in the mouth of a serpent. (63)
No affection for anyone arises on this earth without a prior benefit;
and since peace is attained through giving, the gods become bestowers of one's desires. (64)
The duration of one's existence in the realm of grief is equal to the time during which the gift is being bestowed;
having perceived the exhaustion of the calf’s milk, the mother herself abandons [the calf]. (65)
Furthermore,
[there are] the field, and furthermore, the continuities.
Furthermore, through wholesome and unwholesome karma, the body arises again and again.
A wise person should not destroy fruitless roots or tasks that are impossible to accomplish. (67)
What is beyond the reach of those who speak kindly? Nothing at all. What distance is too great for those who are industrious and capable of managing their own affairs? (68)

As long as this body is healthy, as long as it is free from disease, as long as old age is far off, as long as the power of the senses is unimpeded, and as long as one is capable and not yet exhausted— so long, for the sake of one’s own welfare,
one should exert a great effort while [the opportunity] is aflame. (69)
What kind of effort is this, like digging a well in one's own house? // 70 //
The house of one without a son is empty; a kinsman is empty when he is without a body. The heart of a fool is empty; for one who does not see the emptiness of all things, everything is empty. (71)
The line inscribed upon the forehead by Hari, Hara, Brahmā, or even the gods cannot be erased.
(72) Words endowed with power are to be accepted, even if they come from a child.
Even for the wise, that which is improper must be abandoned by the Lotus-born One.

(73) The accomplishment of desired fruits and the attainment of wealth through cherished desires are what is sought. A man should have [the rite] performed with only two or three kinsmen, not more. (74)
Having eaten, one should sit down; while sitting, one should eat slowly; having eaten, one should lie down comfortably.
One should exert oneself while walking...
The suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap* when it follows a verbal root ending in *r*, provided that the root ends in a long vowel or a consonant and is followed by a prefix. (Pāṇini 7.1.37)
A young girl, a newlywed wife, an elderly woman, a pregnant woman, a woman in labor, and an ascetic;
likewise, the elderly among the couple [should eat] the remnants of the meal. (76)
The fruit of perfection.
From eating [unwholesome] food, from excessive talking, from staying awake at night out of passion, and from the suppression of urine and feces—through these six causes, diseases arise. (77)
Mounting bulls, elephants, palaces, mountain peaks, and trees; smearing oneself with excrement;
weeping excessively; and likewise, approaching those who should not be approached—these are auspicious. (1)

Mounting thorns, bulls, vehicles, goats, camels, and donkeys; seeing half-bodies; and the sight of dogs, crows, snakes, young calves, jackals, deer, and the like—these are inauspicious when seen in public. (2)
If one mounts a donkey, a camel, a buffalo, or a tiger in a dream,
it is certain that death will occur for that person within six months. (3)
A dream occurring in the first watch of the night bears fruit in one year;
in the second, in eight months; in the third, in three months;
and at the time of sunrise, it yields fruit within ten days.
At the time of releasing the cows, it shall immediately yield sevenfold fruit. || 79 ||
If the sun were to rise in the western quarter;
if Mount Meru were to move; if fire were to attain the state of coldness;
(80) and if a lotus were to bloom upon a rock at the summit of a mountain.
That which has been spoken by the wise becomes a falsehood. || 81 ||
In matters of austerity, duty, knowledge, and discipline, one should not be devoid of wonder; for this earth is beautiful, possessing many jewels. (82)
Gambling is the sport of the Asuras... (i.25a, l.1) ...whose women are for sale.
The seven great purifications are indeed constant; the Buddha is one whose intellect is straightforward. 83.
What could it not accomplish?
... the intellect of [those] who follow all [objects]. 84.
To speak what is pleasant as described above is a transgression against the virtuous; for it is the very nature of the wicked that they regard faults as virtues. (85)
In whatever way the mind is, in that same way is speech; thus the fourfold activity of the virtuous is of a single form in both mind and vocal action. (86)
Rāhu constantly exerts his strength, and Ketu diminishes the family;
yet, by your grace, O Lord, may they all always bring about prosperity and remain favorable to us—how wonderful! (87)

The Sun possesses solar valor; the Moon is the very path of Indra; Mars is the source of auspiciousness; Mercury possesses excellent intellect; Jupiter possesses gravity; Venus is pure and white; and Saturn bestows auspicious fortune. (88)
When the Sun is in the *Ārdrā* mansion, Mars and Venus are in *Rohiṇī*, and Saturn is in the *Śakaṭa* (the Cart) mansion— the twelfth— then, for twelve days,
the rain-cloud certainly does not pour down rain. (89)
The steady jewel that opens the bolt of heaven is possessed by one filled with remorse;
he is consumed by the fire of grief as he ages. Rohiṇī [is... pierced by the sharpness of the sun’s rays... 90. (l.3) ...the rising moon... sat.
What could he say? For in the ocean of water, all worldly conditions (upādhi) have reached their complete exhaustion. 90.
Just as this weak conjunction of Śakra with Rohiṇī divides [the rains], so for twelve years it does not rain. 91.
Misfortune is unstable, life-breaths are unstable, and even the body is unstable;
that which is moving is unstable, and what dharma is there that is stable? (92)
In the two [realms], there is a foot and a fourfold velocity; that which pertains to humanity is the fruit of the waves of water. 93.
He makes a womb with a steady mind for the purpose of ascending to heaven;
yet afterwards, joined by that [womb], aged by old age, he is consumed by the fire of grief. (94) He ascends the funeral pyre in the womb of a corpse... [mṛta... yonau samārohet... tāśanam].
... with a mind possessed by passion, [he] goes to the heavenly world.
(95) Just as when the husband has died in the fire, the wife should cause herself to be cremated; for that long he does not release her... [this] worship is most weighty. (95)
She who follows her husband goes again to the three lineages— the maternal, the paternal, and that in which she is conceived.
There are thirty-five million hairs upon the body.
For as long as she lives in this world, she goes to a state of suffering;
whether he be of evil conduct or of good conduct, she must serve her husband, even if he is intent on every kind of sin.
"O Tārā, among these dharmas that are like a wife... 98.

For those women who are deprived of their husbands and whose noble lives have become fruitless— O Lord of the World, such a body is as useless as a wood-apple tree in a cremation ground. (99) A woman who is abandoned by her many sons and kinsmen is to be consumed [as food].
Let her be a woman deprived of a husband, practicing austerities.
(100) A husband who is poor, burdened by calamity, aged, diseased, deformed, fallen, or even miserly—such a man is the ultimate resort for women. (101)
There is no kinsman equal to a husband; there is no friend equal to a husband; there is no [relative] equal to a husband—[he is] united with the husband. 102.
There is no other suffering for ascetics equal to the pain of being separated from one's possessions...
[depositing...
She dies in front of her husband. || 103 ||
Whoever seeks the gods in this manner, even though they have begun [the sacrifice], let him not satisfy the twice-born with [that] imperishable [offering]. 104.
The Nītisāraśloka is completed. Salutations to Śiva. Oṃ.
In the first enclosure: Oṃ soṃ, homage to Īśāna, the source of the world!
Oṃ seṃ, homage to Tatpuruṣa, the source of speech!
Oṃ suṃ ka...saṃ viśva... (l. 2).
Oṃ siṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, the source of Rudra. Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta, the source of Brahmā.

Oṃ saṃ siṃ suṃ seṃ soṃ ... (l. 3) *bhuvat* bhuve namaḥ. In the second enclosure (*varaṇa*), [the deity] named Jayanta, [residing] in the Aśvinī [nakṣatra], in the Kṛttikās, [is] Trasajjaka. Tara, Bhūtapati, Senī, Guha, Saṃjñāka, Hemaśūla, Viśālākṣi, ... Vajradhara ... (l. 5) ... in the third enclosure. Thus: Oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ. Oṃ maṃ mahāvamayai, oṃ maṃ ... (l. 6)
Oṃ gaṃ, homage to Gajendra.
Oṃ suṃ, homage to Sudeha.
Oṃ suṃ, homage to Sumukha.
Oṃ suṃ... (i.28a,
l.1) ...having thoroughly worshipped Indra and the others in the fivefold enclosure, as well as Vajra and the others (l.2).

In the first enclosure are Vaktra, Pralambauṣṭha, Vighneśa, Guṇādhipa, Vinayaka, Dvibhuja, [Khala]. The second enclosure is likewise; the third enclosure consists of Suprabhūta, Suvaktra, Polaka, and Ugra.
Kumbhodara, as well as the fourfold enclosure [consisting of] Indra, Agni... (l. 5)... Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, as well as Īśāna, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu.

In the fivefold enclosure... (l. 6)... the ten weapons are: the spear (*śakti*), the staff (*daṇḍa*), the sword (*khaḍga*), the noose (*pāśa*), as well as the banner (*dhvaja*), the mace (*gadā*), the trident (*śūla*), the lotus (*padma*), and the discus (*cakra*).

...and one should worship Māhīnī, who bestows grace upon her devotees, the witness of all, the protector of the universe, seated upon a steady lotus, Śrī... (l. 2) ...the Goddess who grants success to the entire world.
(l. 3) ...the first enclosure [consists of] Ananta and others; the second enclosure [consists of] Nandin and others; the third enclosure [consists of] Indra and others, with the *vajra*...
